cards.front: First-line vasopressor in septic shock: noradrenaline. If inadequate response, add [___] (works via V1 receptors).
cards.context:
Catecholamine alpha-1 receptors become progressively desensitised after prolonged high-dose stimulation, so escalating a single agent eventually plateaus on MAP.

Adding a non-catecholamine that acts through V1 receptors (vasopressin) restores tone via a parallel pathway, and lets the noradrenaline dose come down.

cards.front: For a 70 kg patient receiving lignocaine with adrenaline (max [___] mg/kg), the total maximum dose is 490 mg.
cards.context:
Adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction, which slows lignocaine systemic absorption — lifting the safe maximum from 3 mg/kg (plain) to 7 mg/kg (with adrenaline).

Adrenaline-containing solutions are contraindicated in end-arterial territories (digits, nose, penis, ears) where vasoconstriction risks ischaemia.

cards.front: Ideal ETT position on CXR: 3-5 cm above the carina (T3-T4 level). Most common malposition is [___] mainstem intubation.
cards.context:
Right mainstem intubation is the most common ETT malposition because the right main bronchus diverges at a smaller angle from the trachea (25° vs 45° for the left).

Head flexion advances the ETT ~2 cm; extension withdraws it ~2 cm.

cards.front: First-line treatment for torsades de pointes is IV magnesium at a dose of [___] g.
cards.context:
Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT in the setting of QT prolongation — the QRS complexes 'twist' around the isoelectric baseline, alternating positive and negative deflections.

Also: stop QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron, hydroxychloroquine), correct K⁺ to >4.5, correct Mg²⁺ to >1.0, isoprenaline or pacing to overdrive >100/min if recurrent.

cards.front: The vital sign that rises earliest in deterioration and is most often omitted from observations is the [___].
cards.context: RR rises early in sepsis, PE, pulmonary oedema, and metabolic acidosis. Yet it's the most frequently omitted vital sign — always count it for a full 60 seconds.

cards.front: Respiratory acidosis HCO₃⁻ compensation: acute = [___] per 10 mmHg pCO₂ rise. Chronic = 4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg.
cards.context:
Acute compensation is minimal (just buffering) because kidneys haven't had time to retain bicarbonate. Chronic compensation (days to weeks) allows kidneys to retain significant bicarbonate, partially normalising pH.

Example: COPD patient with pCO₂ 70 (up 30) → HCO₃⁻ rises ~12 to 36.

cards.front: Normal ABG: pH 7.35–7.45, pCO₂ [___] mmHg, HCO₃ 22–26 mmol/L.
cards.context:
Anchor on 7.4 / 40 / 24. VBG offsets: pH ~0.03 lower, pCO₂ ~6 higher, HCO₃ same.

VBG cannot assess PaO₂.

cards.front: Second-line for status epilepticus after benzodiazepine is [___] at 18 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes.
cards.context:
If benzos fail (~30% of cases), phenytoin 18-20 mg/kg IV blocks voltage-gated sodium channels to stabilise hyperexcitable neurons.

Extravasation causes 'purple glove syndrome' (severe tissue necrosis from the propylene glycol diluent), so use a large-bore IV with saline flush.

cards.front: Anion gap formula: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Normal range is [___] mmol/L.
cards.context:
The anion gap captures unmeasured anions — primarily albumin (~2.4 mmol/L per 10 g/L), with phosphate, lactate, ketones, and toxin metabolites filling the rest in disease.

Without the correction, a sepsis patient with albumin of 20 looks like 'normal AG' when they actually have a meaningful HAGMA.

cards.front: Pre-anaesthetic fasting: [___] hours for clear fluids and 6 hours for solids.
cards.context:
GA abolishes protective airway reflexes. Gastric contents can regurgitate, causing pulmonary aspiration leading to chemical pneumonitis, ARDS, or death.

Standard fasting: 6 hours for solids, 2 hours for clear fluids — the '2-and-6 rule.'.

cards.front: F in FASTHUG BID = Feeding (NOT fluids). Start enteral nutrition within [___] hours.
cards.context: Students reflexively say 'Fluids' because critically ill patients get lots of IV fluids.

cards.front: The HIET bolus dose for BB/CCB toxicity is insulin [___] IV, given before starting a dextrose-buffered maintenance infusion.
cards.context:
HIET (high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy) for severe BB/CCB toxicity uses 10-20× normal sliding-scale doses.

Standard regimen: bolus 1 U/kg IV, then 0.5-1 U/kg/h infusion with concomitant dextrose to maintain euglycaemia.

Rationale: failing myocardium switches from fatty-acid to glucose metabolism in toxicity, but glucose uptake requires insulin — HIET restores myocardial energy supply and improves contractility.

cards.front: Status epilepticus second-line alternatives: levetiracetam [___] mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g) or valproate 40 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes.
cards.context: Status epilepticus second-line: levetiracetam is increasingly preferred over phenytoin as it has fewer drug interactions, no cardiac toxicity, and doesn't require slow infusion or monitoring.

cards.front: Therapeutic LMWH must be stopped at least [___] hours before neuraxial anaesthesia.
cards.context:
Therapeutic LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD, dalteparin 200 IU/kg) requires 24 hours off before neuraxial — about 4-5 half-lives, enough to ensure peak anti-Xa activity has cleared.

If anti-Xa monitoring is available (which it usually isn't in routine ED/anaesthetics), confirm levels are <0.1-0.2 IU/mL pre-procedure.

cards.front: Normal potassium (K⁺) range is [___] mmol/L.
cards.context:
Serum K⁺ 3.5-5.0 mmol/L — narrow range matters because K⁺ sets the resting membrane potential of every excitable cell (cardiac myocytes most vulnerable).

Hypokalaemia (<3.5): muscle weakness, ileus, U waves, ↑ventricular ectopy, ↑digoxin sensitivity. Hyperkalaemia (>5.5): peaked T waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS, sine wave → asystole.

cards.front: A delta ratio detects [___] metabolic disorders.
cards.context: A delta ratio outside 0.8-2.0 reveals that there is more than one acid-base process occurring simultaneously — e.g., DKA (high AG) plus diarrhoea (normal AG), or lactic acidosis plus vomiting (alkalosis).

cards.front: Digoxin Fab indications: life-threatening [___] or hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L).
cards.context:
Digoxin blocks Na/K-ATPase pumps → intracellular sodium rises → cardiac arrhythmias. Extracellular potassium also rises (pump failure) → hyperkalaemia.

Both are indications for urgent Fab.

cards.front: Using Parkland (4 mL x kg x %TBSA), give [___] of the total in the first 8 hours from time of injury.
cards.context:
Parkland gives 24-hour burn resuscitation: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA, half over first 8 h (from time of injury, NOT presentation), half over next 16. Clock starts at injury — critical for transfers.

Worked example: 80 kg, 40% TBSA → 4 × 80 × 40 = 12,800 mL over 24 h; first 8 h = 6,400 mL (800 mL/h). If presenting 2 h post-burn, deliver 6,400 mL over remaining 6 h = 1,067 mL/h.

cards.front: 4% dextrose + 0.18% saline is ideal maintenance because 2.5 L delivers ~74 mmol Na — matching [___] daily requirements.
cards.context: For a 70kg patient, daily needs are ~2500mL water and 75mmol sodium. 4% dextrose + 0.18% saline delivers exactly this — it's physiologically designed maintenance, not resuscitation.

cards.front: Status epilepticus second-line alternatives: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g) or valproate [___] mg/kg IV over 15 minutes.
cards.context: Status epilepticus second-line: levetiracetam is increasingly preferred over phenytoin as it has fewer drug interactions, no cardiac toxicity, and doesn't require slow infusion or monitoring.

cards.front: Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressors needed for MAP ≥[___] mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.
cards.context:
Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors AND lactate >2 despite adequate fluids. Both criteria must be met.

This subset carries >40% mortality.

cards.front: PCA background infusions increase risk of respiratory depression without improving outcomes. Monitor RR/SpO₂ [___] for first 6-12 hours.
cards.context:
PCA allows patient autonomy over opioid dosing. Background infusions are NOT routinely used — they don't improve outcomes and increase respiratory depression risk.

Monitoring is critical: hourly for first 6-12 hours, then 2-hourly.

cards.front: Target lactate clearance in sepsis is 10-20% within [___] hours; failure prompts reassessment.
cards.context:
Lactate clearance is a downstream check that the resuscitation is actually reaching tissue, not a marker of pure perfusion.

Failure to clear is a prompt to reassess source control (is the abscess drained, the line removed, the antibiotic broad enough?), inotropic need (is there occult septic cardiomyopathy on echo?).

cards.front: Delta ratio 0.8-2.0 indicates pure HAGMA; <0.8 = mixed HAGMA + NAGMA; >2.0 = HAGMA + [___].
cards.context:
In a clean HAGMA, every unmeasured anion consumes a bicarbonate — rise in AG and fall in HCO₃ should be ~1:1. Delta ratio formalises that; value 0.8-2.0 says nothing else is going on.

Outside that window a second process is hiding. <0.8 = HCO₃ fell further than AG rose, so a normal-AG acidosis is co-existing (DKA + diarrhoea.

cards.front: ICU patients who benefit most from stress ulcer prophylaxis are those ventilated over 48 hours or with [___].
cards.context: SUP-ICU (2018) showed PPIs reduce GI bleeding but not mortality, with signals of increased C. difficile and VAP.

cards.front: On CXR, the ETT tip should be at least [___] above the carina in neutral position.
cards.context:
ETT position on CXR should be at least 3 cm above the carina in neutral head position. If the neck is flexed, the ETT advances (towards carina).

If extended, it withdraws. Too low risks right main bronchus intubation.

cards.front: Paediatric fluid resuscitation for shock: [___] mL/kg crystalloid bolus given rapidly over 5-10 minutes.
cards.context:
Paediatric shock fluid resuscitation: 20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% saline) given over 5-10 minutes per bolus. Reassess after each bolus — heart rate, capillary refill, mental status, urine output.

Children compensate longer than adults via tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, then crash suddenly — by the time hypotension appears, they've lost 30-40% of circulating volume.

cards.front: Ottawa Ankle Rules: X-ray if tenderness at posterior lateral or [___] malleolus (distal 6 cm), base of 5th metatarsal, navicular bone, or unable to weight-bear 4 steps.
cards.context: The Ottawa rules check four bony areas plus weight-bearing ability. The midfoot component (base of 5th MT and navicular) is often forgotten but catches important fractures that can be missed clinically.

cards.front: Per CRASH-2, trauma TXA dosing is 1 g IV bolus over 10 min, then the same dose given as an infusion over 8 hours. Beyond [___] hours from injury, the mortality benefit is lost — and may even be harmful.
cards.context:
CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010, n=20,211): TXA cuts all-cause mortality by 1.5% absolute (NNT ~67) when given within 3 hours of injury.

Mechanism: blocks plasminogen activation, preventing fibrinolysis without promoting new clot formation.

Protocol: same dose for bolus (over 10 min) and 8-hour infusion — the symmetry makes it easy to recall under stress.

cards.front: Berlin ARDS severity threshold between severe and moderate is a P/F ratio of [___].
cards.context:
The Berlin definition stratifies ARDS by P/F ratio: mild 200-300, moderate 100-200, severe ≤100 (all with PEEP ≥5).

P/F is calculated on PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O — without that floor, the ratio is unreliable because atelectasis falsely lowers it. The ratio assesses oxygenation efficiency relative to FiO₂.
